purpose: No analyzer may publish a framework capability it does not have, or name one framework twice. The family contract (real-csharp-analyzer.ts CONV-CS-2 header, java sibling) is three metadata keys — `framework` (the deterministic primary pick), `detectedFrameworks` (always an array), `frameworkPatterns` (aligned) — plus the `hasFrameworkIntelligence` capability claim. Registered like the regex debt and like R7: entries are keyed by source statement (not line, because positions move and statements do not) with an exact count, so an added site and a removed one are both deliberate acts.

ooTarget.note: Owner standard: the seven OO lanes must reach zero, lane by lane, with a fixture and a reverting mutant each — never by editing this register. MET as of this phase: ruby (#749 — the unreachable callback trigger, the Rails/Ruby on Rails divergence, the duplicate accumulator and the missing primary pick), pinned by ruby/framework-surface-pins with four caught mutants; python (#747 — the surface was initialized and never written while the capability claim was published on every file), pinned by python/framework-surface-pins with two caught mutants (the trigger surface going dead again, and the emitted order following import order instead of the marker table); swift (#838/#836 — no primary pick, no frameworkPatterns, 81 findings over 248 real corpus files) and objective-c (CONV-OC-1 — no frameworkPatterns, 7 findings over 7 detecting files), each pinned by its own framework-surface-pins fixture and caught mutants; and php, which had the family's only two debts that were *static false negatives* and not violations — the two unreachable markers (`App\` root, bare `TestCase`, #931, each compared against text no call site could pass) and the primary pick following DETECTION order rather than a marker table (#934, python's defect verbatim, carried because this row was already holding the markers and a row holds only what someone measured). Both fixed, each with its own pin and reverting mutant: php/framework-surface-pins + php/framework-app-root catch php/framework-app-root-marker-dead and php/framework-phpunit-base-marker-dead; php/framework-order (document order deliberately the inverse of the table order) catches php/framework-order-document. Laravel's breadth was counted before it was applied — 0 of 4,588 corpus files declare any `App` namespace — and `namespace App;` alone still deliberately does not fire.

runtimeOwed: NARROWED 2026-09-24 (#931 fixed): the runtime half has been run over 1,653 real files and reads ZERO contract findings on BOTH halves — the analyzers, and the object `ASTEngine.parseFile` publishes. What is still owed, and is why this field is not deleted: the corpus draw does NOT exercise every registered static shape. After the fix, the bare-`TestCase` branch IS exercised (the 29-file delta above, every one opened by hand); the php `App\`-root marker is NOT — 0 files of the draw declare any `namespace App\...`, so its witness is the fixture `php/framework-app-root` and the grammar-level marker probe, not a corpus file. A static shape with no runtime witness is a shape whose severity is inferred; it is recorded here rather than implied by the clean corpus row.

Adding it convicted 7 files; scoping it to the exercised contract (a non-empty detection) was forced by a measurement — the strict per-file reading convicted 189 of 190 real rake/rack files for omitting `framework`/`frameworkPatterns` on files where nothing was detected, a shape with no consumer-visible effect because the pipeline writes all three keys anyway.

python PRE-FIX, kept as the measurement the fix answers: `frameworks: {}` was initialized and never written while the emit block published `hasFrameworkIntelligence: true` unconditionally on every file, including `x = 1`; the corpus read 0 detecting files of 187. Now a marker table read from the AST publishes the pick, and the corpus reads 7 detecting files with 0 findings.
ruby PRE-FIX, kept as the measurement the fix answers: duplicated `Ruby on Rails` on a real corpus file (rack/test.rb, 3 identical entries) and no primary pick — 2 runtime findings, now 0.

php PRE-FIX, kept as the measurement the fix answers: two registered markers were compared against text no call site could pass — the `App\` root against a namespace string ENDING in a backslash (`text === "App\"`, an exact match on a separator no node carries) and the bare `TestCase` against the NAMESPACE text while the base clause was never handed to the detector at all. Both cases read MISS against their own `expectDetected` while R8 read MET over the corpora, because a marker that cannot fire is a detector every corpus calls clean. Now 23/23 cases behave, 0 claim misses.

php BREADTH, counted rather than assumed. The Laravel rule was widened to `App\`-PREFIX and the count taken BEFORE applying it: 0 of 4,588 files across php's two M14 corpora declare any `App` namespace, and `namespace App;` alone still deliberately does not fire (asserted by php/framework-app-root, which also pins the negative). The bare-`TestCase` rule was counted AFTER and opened file by file, because its evidence is a NAME: php's corpus row moved 21 -> 50 detecting files, all 29 new ones `slim/tests/*.php`, all genuinely PHPUnit tests — 24 import the base, and 5 resolve `TestCase` to their own namespace's `Slim\Tests\TestCase`, which is `abstract class TestCase extends PhpUnitTestCase` with `use PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase as PhpUnitTestCase`. Zero false positives observed; the residual risk is stated, not hidden: a project whose own base class is called `TestCase` and is NOT PHPUnit's would be one, and the analyzer reports the name match, not the resolved class.

php PRIMARY PICK PRE-FIX, the third debt on the same row: the lane published `framework: [...detectedFrameworks][0]` — a Set's INSERTION order, i.e. whichever marker fired first in the file — so the primary pick depended on the statement layout of one file. That is python's defect verbatim, named in this register; swift/objc/csharp all carry an ORDER table and php carried none. Now PHP_FRAMEWORK_ORDER, with unmatched names APPENDED rather than dropped. Corpus effect: none of the 4,588 files change their published surface (identical framework, detectedFrameworks and counts), which is why php/framework-order exists — its document order is deliberately the INVERSE of the table order, so the pre-fix reading is what a regression reproduces (php/framework-order-document, CAUGHT).

ruby FALSE POSITIVE, the third debt on the same seam: `detectRubyFrameworks` fired "rspec" on a BARE `describe ` substring, and rack's test/ directory is minitest/spec — test/helper.rb requires 'minitest/global_expectations/autorun', the Gemfile and gemspec carry no rspec at all, and the analyzer's own comments call these files minitest specs. Measured 36 of 190 pinned-corpus files publishing ["rspec"] with ZERO requiring rspec: 0 true / 36 false is a false detector, and the corpus half could not convict it because framework-intelligence runs only in the published seam — the same blindness that let #932 live. Fixed by removing the bare trigger (require 'rspec' kept, positive control added; require 'hanami' added as the last item of #749's named list, 0 corpus cost measured). ruby's published row: 37 -> 1 detecting files, all 36 removed detections false.

publishedPayload.note: the same files through ASTEngine.parseFile — the object a consumer actually receives. RE-MEASURED 2026-09-24: 1,650 files, 512 with detection, 0 findings, and the seam now has an assertion of its own — ruby published ["Ruby on Rails","rails"] for ONE framework because enhanceWithFrameworkIntelligence unions its own slug vocabulary with the analyzer's, so the analyzer half could never see it (#932, fixed in framework-intelligence.ts). The new case runs through ASTEngine.parseFile and is proven load-bearing: reverting the alias flips it to MISS and the probe to 22/23.
publishedPayload.openClass: NONE OPEN. The 70 findings above were the only real published findings this half has ever reported once its A3 stopped convicting the pipeline's documented no-detection default; the three candidate resolutions were put to the owner, who chose the pipeline alignment.
